---
title: "A recipe the agent can follow"
---

Every app you created this year arrived with a folder you have probably never
opened. It sits next to `src/` and it is called `.agents/skills/`. The SVG part
named it once and promised that a later part would have you write a skill of
your own. This chapter opens the folder, watches the one skill inside it change
how your buddy answers, and then writes that skill for the salon app.

## The skill that was already in your project {#sec-skills-experiment}

1. Open `coursework/hairdresser`, the salon from @sec-queues-exercise, and open
   `.agents/skills/find-docs/SKILL.md`. The file starts with a block between
   two `---` lines:

   ```yaml
   ---
   name: find-docs
   description: >-
     Retrieves up-to-date documentation, API references, and code examples for any
     developer technology. Use this skill whenever the user asks about a specific
     library, framework, SDK, CLI tool, or cloud service ...
   ---
   ```

2. Read the rest of the file. It is one page of instructions for the agent: two
   commands, `npx ctx7@latest library <name> "<query>"` and
   `npx ctx7@latest docs <libraryId> "<query>"`, the order they go in, and a
   rule that says three tries per question and no more.

3. Start `pi` in the project and ask it a question about a library:

   > Which Playwright assertion checks how many elements a locator matches?

   Watch the tool lines above the answer instead of the answer itself. The
   agent reads `.agents/skills/find-docs/SKILL.md`, then runs the two commands
   it found in there, and answers after that. Some runs answer straight away
   without opening the file. Put `/skill:find-docs` in front of your question
   and it opens it.

4. Run the first of those two commands yourself:

   ```bash
   npx ctx7@latest library Playwright "assertion to check how many elements a locator matches"
   ```

   ```text
   1. Title: Playwright
      Context7-compatible library ID: /microsoft/playwright
      Description: Playwright is a framework for Web Testing and Automation, enabling cross-browser testing of Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit with a single API.
      Code Snippets: 6438
      Source Reputation: High
      Benchmark Score: 85.72
      Versions: v1.51.0, v1.58.2, v1.61.0
   ```

   Four more entries follow. Take the id from the first one and ask for the
   documentation itself:

   ```bash
   npx ctx7@latest docs /microsoft/playwright "locator count assertion toHaveCount"
   ```

   ````text
   ### Assert element count with toHaveCount

   Source: https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/docs/src/api/class-locatorassertions.md

   Ensures the locator resolves to an exact number of DOM nodes. Use this to verify the size of a collection or list.

   ```javascript
   const list = page.locator('list > .component');
   await expect(list).toHaveCount(3);
   ```
   ````

   The same entry follows in Java, Python, and C#, and every entry carries the
   `Source:` line with it.

5. Close `pi` and start it again with its skills switched off, then ask exactly
   the same question:

   ```bash
   pi --no-skills
   ```

Both answers say `toHaveCount`, and yours very likely did too. What changed is
where the answer came from. The second one came out of the model's memory of the
internet as it looked during training. The first one came with a link to the
page in the Playwright repository that says so today, which is the difference
between an answer you can check and an answer you have to believe.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The first start in a folder

`pi` asks whether it may use the files of the project you started it in, and
skills from `.agents/skills/` stay switched off until you say yes. Say no and
the agent still works, it just never sees the recipes. A project you did not
write yourself is worth a look before you answer that question, because a skill
file tells the agent what to do and the agent does it.
:::

## What a skill is {#sec-skills-what}

A **skill** is a folder with a `SKILL.md` file in it, and that file is a recipe
for one kind of task. The folders live in `.agents/skills/` in the project, so
they travel with the repository, and every agent that reads the
[Agent Skills standard](https://agentskills.io/specification) finds them there.
Your own machine-wide recipes go into `.agents/skills/` in your home folder
instead.

The `name` and the `description` from the top of the file are the only part the
model sees all the time. Everything below the second `---` line is on disk and
nowhere else until the agent decides to read it, which it does when your task
sounds like the description. That is why `find-docs` spends five lines on
describing when to use it and names React, Prisma, and Django in there: the
description is not a label, it is the trigger.

So a lazy description costs you the whole skill. "Helps with tests" matches
nothing in particular, the agent never opens the file, and you sit there
wondering why your recipe changed nothing.

## What a year of AGENTS.md looks like {#sec-skills-agents-md}

`AGENTS.md` in the project root is the other half. It has no trigger and no
description, because the agent reads all of it before it starts working, every
single time.

Yours has grown line by line since the SVG part: the rule that a changed script
in `package.json` also changes `README.md` (@sec-toolchain-assets-agents), the
course style, and the sentence from the testing part that says to run
`npm run verify` before reporting success and to quote what it printed
(@sec-verify-ci-agents). A good `AGENTS.md` for the salon holds four kinds of
thing, and it is shorter than you expect:

```markdown
# Salon waiting line

A page where humans and dogs join a waiting line and get served in the order
they arrived.

## Layout

- `src/customer.ts` holds the abstract `Customer` and every customer type.
- `src/waiting-line.ts` holds the generic `WaitingLine<T>` and its `Node<T>`.
- `src/index.ts` only wires the page.

## Commands

- `npm test` runs the unit tests.
- `npm run verify` runs `tsc --noEmit`, Biome, and the tests. Run it before you
  report that you are done, and say what it printed.

## Rules

- Course style: single quotes, semicolons, `querySelector<T>` with a null check
  that throws, fields as `private readonly` parameter properties.
- `WaitingLine<T>` stays generic. It never mentions `Customer`.
- No `instanceof` and no `switch` on a type field. Different behavior per
  customer type is an overridden `describe()`.
```

Layout, commands, rules, and the fourth kind: the things this agent got wrong in
this project before. That last group is the one nobody writes and everybody
needs. When your buddy puts a class into `index.ts` twice in one week, the fix
is one line in `AGENTS.md`, not a third reminder in the chat that you throw away
when the session ends.

The line between the two files is the trigger. A rule that is true for every
task belongs in `AGENTS.md`. A procedure for one kind of task belongs in a
skill, where it stays out of the way until that task shows up.

## Writing a recipe of your own {#sec-skills-recipe}

The salon needs one recipe more than any other: adding a class. You did it for
`Human` and for `Dog`, and the next customer type works the same way. Ask the
buddy for one and you get a class that runs. What you get around it is a coin
flip, because nothing in the task says which file it goes in, whether a test
comes with it, or where the job ends.

A recipe has three parts, and the file below has them in order. When to use it,
the steps in the order they happen, and the checks that say whether the job is
done. Create `.agents/skills/tested-class/SKILL.md` in the salon project:

```markdown
---
name: tested-class
description: Adds a class to this project together with its unit tests. Use when a task asks for a new customer type, a new class, or a new model file under src/.
---

# A new class with tests

## When to use this

Use this recipe when the task asks for a new class: a new customer type, a new
model, anything that ends up as a `class` under `src/`. Do not use it for
changes to the page, the CSS, or a class that already exists.

## Steps

1. Decide where the class goes. A new member of the `Customer` family belongs
   in `src/customer.ts`. Anything else gets its own module `src/<name>.ts`,
   kebab-case in the file name.

2. Write the test file first: `src/<name>.test.ts`, next to the class file.
   One `describe` per class, one `it` per behavior, and the name of an `it`
   reads as a sentence.

3. Run `npx vitest run src/<name>.test.ts` and read the failure. A test that is
   green before the class exists is testing nothing.

4. Write the class. Extend the abstract base class when the family has one,
   take the fields as `private readonly` parameter properties, and give
   different behavior through an overridden method, never through `instanceof`.

5. Run `npm run verify` and put the test counts from its output into your
   answer.

6. Stop at the model. `index.html`, `src/styles.css`, and `src/index.ts` change
   only when the task asks for the page.

## Before you report that you are done

- The test file sits next to the class file and carries the same base name.
- `npm run verify` printed no findings, and the number of tests is higher than
  it was before you started.
- Nothing outside `src/` changed unless the task asked for it.
```

Read the steps again and notice how little of it is about TypeScript. Step 1
answers a question the agent cannot guess, step 3 makes it prove the test can
fail, and step 6 draws a border it kept walking over. Those are your rules for
your project, written down once instead of typed into a chat every Tuesday.

The checks at the bottom do a job of their own. An agent that reports "done" has
told you nothing, and an agent that reports "verify printed 17 tests, one more
than before" has handed you a number you can look at yourself.

## One recipe, many projects {#sec-skills-lock}

A skill is a folder with text in it, so copying one into another project is
`cp -r` and nothing else. That is how `find-docs` got into your starter: someone
copied it from the repository of the people who wrote it, and the note about
where it came from is in `skills-lock.json` in the project root:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "skills": {
    "find-docs": {
      "source": "upstash/context7",
      "sourceType": "github",
      "skillPath": "skills/find-docs/SKILL.md",
      "computedHash": "93ec2d2786d7e83973252383875c4f345a2ee7cbbd08a1ab38e5201b214640ee"
    }
  }
}
```

The file records where each borrowed skill came from and a hash of the text as
it arrived. Half a year later that answers two questions you cannot answer from
the folder alone: whether a newer version exists upstream, and whether the copy
in your project is still the original or something a classmate edited. Your own
`tested-class` gets no entry, because nobody borrowed it. It is yours, and
`git log` is its history.

::: {.research title="Two git commands the exercise needs"}
The exercise below asks the buddy for the same feature twice, once without your
recipe and once with it, and you compare the two attempts. That needs a way to
see what the agent changed, and a way to get back to where you started. Neither
is in this chapter.

1. Which git command shows you the lines that changed in your project since the
   last commit, and what do the `+` and `-` at the start of those lines mean?
   The git documentation for that command answers both halves. `git status`,
   which you have used since the git chapter, keeps its job here: it lists the
   files, and the new command shows the lines inside them.
2. You want the project back exactly as it was at the last commit. One command
   throws away your changes to files git already knows, and a second one deletes
   the files that were never committed. Name both, and say which of the two can
   destroy work that has never been saved anywhere. The git documentation has a
   page for each of them.

Keep the commands in your head rather than in a bookmark. The moment you need
them is the moment an agent has rewritten a file you liked, and that is a bad
moment to start searching.
:::

## Exercise: two attempts at the same cat {#sec-skills-exercise}

The salon takes cats now. You ask the buddy for the class twice, from the same
starting point, and let the two attempts argue for themselves.

1. Open `coursework/hairdresser`, run `npm run verify`, and commit whatever is
   still open. `git status` has to print "nothing to commit, working tree clean"
   before you go on, because everything below compares your project against that
   commit.

2. **Attempt one, without a recipe.** Start the buddy with its skills switched
   off:

   ```bash
   pi --no-skills
   ```

   Ask for the new customer type in one sentence:

   > Add a Cat customer type. A cat has a name and a breed, and describes itself
   > as 🐈 Mimi (Siamese).

3. Look at what came back, with `git status` for the file names and your first
   research answer for the lines inside them. Two questions, and neither of them
   is "does it look nice": which files did the agent touch, and is a new test
   file among them? Then run `npm run verify` yourself and read the last two
   lines, because the test count answers a third question the file names
   cannot.

4. Put the project back on the last commit with the two commands from your
   second research answer, then check with `git status` that nothing is left
   over. A forgotten file from attempt one lands in the middle of attempt two
   and ruins the comparison.

5. **Write the recipe.** Create `.agents/skills/tested-class/SKILL.md` with the
   three parts from @sec-skills-recipe: when to use it, the steps, the checks.
   Type it yourself rather than pasting the chapter's version, and change the
   steps where your salon works differently from the one in the text. The
   description is the part to spend real time on, because it decides whether the
   file is ever read.

6. **Attempt two, with the recipe.** Start `pi` normally and send exactly the
   same sentence as in step 2. Watch the first tool line: an agent that picked
   the recipe up reads `SKILL.md` before it touches any of your files. If it
   does not, `/skill:tested-class` loads the recipe by hand, and a description
   that needed forcing is a description worth rewriting.

7. Compare the two attempts against the three questions from step 3, then decide
   which one you would commit. Both attempts can be good. Judge them on whether
   the rules you wrote held: a test file written before the class, a test count
   that went up, and files outside `src/` that stayed untouched while the task
   never mentioned the page.

8. Keep the better attempt and throw the other away. Then go through every line
   you kept and say out loud what it does, to the person next to you or to the
   buddy itself. A line you cannot explain does not get committed.

9. **Teach the project what you learned.** Somewhere in those two runs the
   agent did something you had to correct. Put it into `AGENTS.md` as one
   sentence in your own words, next to the rules that are already in there. If
   both attempts really were clean, write the rule for the thing you fixed by
   hand instead.

10. Run `npm run verify`, then commit the kept change together with
    `SKILL.md` and `AGENTS.md`. Expected result: green, and one test more than
    the verify run in step 1 printed.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The same prompt twice

The same model with the same prompt does not answer the same way twice, so
attempt one might write a beautiful test file without any recipe at all, and
attempt two might still wander into `index.html`. Neither result makes your
recipe pointless or magic. A rule you wrote down is a rule you can point at when
the agent skips it, and "you did not follow step 3 of tested-class" is a
sentence that fixes a session in five seconds.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early

**Take the recipe with you.** Copy `.agents/skills/tested-class/` into
`coursework/train-builder` or into whichever project from Part 7 you kept, edit
the file-layout step to match that project, and ask for a small class there.
Nothing else has to change, and nothing gets added to `skills-lock.json`,
because the recipe never came from anywhere but you.

**A second recipe.** The salon has one more job with steps worth writing down:
adding a control to the page. Write `page-control` with the steps
you actually follow, from the `<label for>` in `index.html` to the null check in
`src/index.ts`, and let the buddy add a Serve all button with it.
:::
